newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba stages huge May Day parade.
newsitem.headline: Cuba stages huge May Day parade.

text.p: Hundreds of thousands of Cubans marched through Havana's Revolution Square on Thursday in a huge May Day parade staged by Cuba's rulers as a show of support for one-party communism and a protest against U.S. policy.

The march, one of the traditional set pieces in Cuba's political calendar, was also dedicated to the 30th anniversary of the death of Ernesto "Che" Guevara, Argentine guerrilla leader and hero of Cuba's Revolution, in the Bolivian jungle.

With patriotic songs blaring from loudspeakers, and under the gaze of a large mural of Guevara, a huge column of workers carrying placards of revolutionary slogans advanced from Havana's Paseo Avenue into the square.

Cuban President Fidel Castro, wearing his trademark green military uniform and cap, watched the parade. The 70-year-old leader, who was flanked by other senior government officials, looked tired and haggard.

Organisers of the Havana May Day march had said they expected more than one million of the capital's more than two million residents to take part. Smaller marches took place in provincial capitals across the communist-ruled island.

Pedro Ross, head of Cuba's official trade union, Central de Trabajadores de Cuba (CTC), set the tone of the Havana march, asking in a crowd-rousing speech: "Will the (U.S.) imperialists, with their blockade, with their Helms-Burton law, with their attacks of every kind, snatch away from us our independence, our revolution or our socialism?"

Authorities billed the march as a protest against hostile U.S. government policy towards Cuba, especially the U.S. Helms-Burton law that seeks to tighten a 35-year economic embargo to force the island to abandon communist rule.
"There will never be a counter-revolutionary transition in Cuba," Ross said. He said eight million of Cuba's 11 million inhabitants had signed a declaration against the U.S. law.

Havana residents had been summoned to the well-organised May Day event by a barrage of government propaganda portraying attendance as a patriotic duty. As usual, authorities presented the march as a massive show of support for Cuba's one-party communist system and its leadership.

"This great First of May ... demonstrates how strong the mobilising power of the revolution is," Ross said. He said Cuba, one of the last remaining communist states, would be one of the few nations to celebrate Workers' Day on such a scale.

"The order of the day in today's world of neo-liberal capitalism is economic instability, ungovernability, corruption, unemployment," he said. He listed as a national priority the need to improve economic efficiency as part of an effort to emerge from a severe recession triggered by the collapse of trade and aid ties with the former Soviet bloc.
Another priority, he said, was a campaign to crack down on rising crime and illegal economic activities.

As the march went ahead, mobile anti-aircraft units remained deployed at several points along the capital's seafront, their 23mm cannon pointing northwards towards the United States. No official explanation was given but the units were deployed on occasions in the past to deter the threat of unauthorised incursions by planes or boats crewed by anti-Castro Cuban exiles living in the United States.
